Sports.title: Spurs 3-1 Coventry: James Maddison shines on Tottenham return
Sports.text:
Roberto de Zerbi has used all the tools at his disposal to discover the missing spark in struggling Tottenham Hotspur, from acting as an amateur psychologist to team bonding dinners, then a sunshine break in Marbella.

The answer, at least when Spurs finally moved off the bottom of the table with their first Premier League win this season against Coventry City, came in the shape of James Maddison as he made his first start in 18 months.

He missed most of last season after suffering an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in pre-season, before fracturing his shoulder in the opening-weekend defeat at Brentford in this campaign.

The 29-year-old finally made it back into the Spurs starting line-up to face Coventry - and delivered in spectacular style to set them on the way to a 3-1 victory that De Zerbi hopes will finally give their season lift-off.

Maddison could barely keep the smile from his face as he warmed up, then made his mark in the 14th minute by showing what Spurs have been missing with a brilliant right-foot finish from 20 yards, taking Mohammed Kudus' pass first time to arc a sweeping strike high beyond Coventry City keeper Carl Rushworth.

It was a moment of sweet relief for Maddison, the goal getting loud gasps of admiration from Spurs supporters as it was shown several times on the stadium's big screens.

Even though the goal came against his former club, Maddison celebrated with his trademark imaginary dart throwing motion before kissing the badge on his Spurs shirt.

Maddison's significance to Spurs is illustrated by the fact they had won just 12 out of 57 Premier League games since his last top-flight goal, in a 1-0 victory against Manchester United in February 2025. They had averaged less than a point a game since then.

And since his last start, at Liverpool on 27 April 2025, Spurs had won only 11 of 49 league games in between, losing 23.

Spurs cannot kid themselves that this was a glorious victory. It was actually only their sixth win in the past 37 home league games - drawing 10 and losing 21 - and just their fourth league victory overall in 2026, having played 27, drawn 10 and lost 13.

And it was the first time they scored three goals or more at home in the league since the opening day of last season, when they beat Burnley 3-0 in Thomas Frank's first game in charge.

There are still too many nerves around Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and in De Zerbi's team for calm and relaxation.

The victory margin flattered them somewhat, with Jack Rudoni equalising for Coventry City before Omar Marmoush's strike for his first goal for the club, then another from Ben Davies in stoppage time after a dreadful Rushworth error finally allowed Spurs to enjoy the relief of victory.

And there were other things to celebrate. As well as Maddison's successful return to the starting line-up, there was the sight of Dejan Kulusevski finally back as an 87th-minute replacement for Kudus after 526 days out with a knee injury.

Maddison got a deserved standing ovation when he was substituted for Conor Gallagher after 69 minutes, but the reception for Kulusevski was arguably even more rapturous as he finally took to the pitch again after such a long battle to regain fitness.

It was Maddison, however, who claimed the major plaudits after he was the driving force behind the win that has proved so elusive - his positive approach playing with a smile on his face provides refreshment of its own after such a depressing sequence of results.

He was eager to get on the ball, was constantly probing and prompting, all before he inevitably tired after the break.

"I spoke to the gaffer this weekend about it, feeling like it was the right moment for me to go back into the starting XI after a bit of a stop-start start to the season," Maddison told Sky Sports.

"I just wanted to play well and show my abilities, show what the team has missed the last 18 months. The gaffer asked me to play and wanted to enjoy watching from the side. Hopefully I did that, and a goal is always nice."

If his aim was to show what Spurs have been missing, this was very much mission accomplished.

And as well as Maddison and Kulusevski, Marmoush will gain confidence from his strike, another superb curling effort that gave Rushworth no chance.

De Zerbi will know this is only a start, with a tough trip to face Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday evening (17:30 BST).

He welcomed the return of Maddison and Kulusevski, saying: "They are different players, different talents, different personalities. With them in the dressing room there is a different atmosphere."

What changes the atmosphere in the dressing room and beyond most are victories.

Now De Zerbi and Spurs can actually build on three points at last, and the sights of Maddison and Kulusevski back in action will have the Italian hoping they can accelerate an improvement after the misery of recent times.

Gaming_Tech.title: DeepSeek banned from US government in race with China for AI dominance
Gaming_Tech.text:
The US has ordered all artificial intelligence (AI) technology from the Chinese firm DeepSeek to be removed from most government systems.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has banned all use of DeepSeek within civilian government agencies, and any technology built with the aid of its AI models.

As a powerful AI model that is open source - meaning it is free to access and less expensive to use - DeepSeek has been seen as a disruptive force in the ongoing AI technology race.

While the DHS notice did not detail the exact security concerns surrounding DeepSeek, the White House has this year criticised AI firms from China.

The DHS, DeepSeek, and the Chinese embassy in Washington DC have been contacted for comment.

The DHS made the order public on Monday, but the ban took effect from the end of July.

The order is specific to civilian agencies, including the Department of the Treasury, the Department of State and the Department of Justice. However, agencies within the Department of Defense are excluded.

The ban follows criticism of Chinese AI from the Trump administration, and from American firms.

White House tech lead Michael Kratsios wrote earlier this year in an internal memo that "malicious exploitation" of American AI firms had been occurring, mainly by rival firms in China.

Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which are poised to list on the public stock market in the coming months, have also claimed to have had their AI models essentially copied by some Chinese AI firms, including DeepSeek.

US president Donald Trump has made clear that he sees China as the key US rival when it comes to development of AI, something he sees as crucial to the future of the country.

DeepSeek has grown in popularity since its initial public release in 2025, with models being in such demand that the company's servers have gone down at times.

While DeepSeek's free chatbot app is one of the most downloaded apps in the Apple App Store rankings, its AI models are also used by US tech companies. Companies like Snowflake, Vercel and OpenRouter all incorporate DeepSeek in their offerings to customers.

Startups have flocked to open source models like DeepSeek.

For a technology or AI developer, using DeepSeek in their work costs a fraction of what a closed model like Google's Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude or OpenAI's Codex would.

Similarly, the expense borne by DeepSeek to develop its models has been astronomically less than what it has cost US AI firms to develop their own.

Last year, DeepSeek said it took about $6m (£4.5m) to train the debut version of its model, while the costs associated with OpenAI's GPT-4 were roughly $100m. Such revelations sent tech stocks tumbling.

The most recent version of DeepSeek was released last week. Users of the model have praised it online, saying it beats even the most advanced AI tools out of OpenAI on common tasks for AI tools like computer software coding.

Gaming_Tech.title: Shane Lowry: Irish golfer links up with Rory McIlroy in first ever TGL trade
Gaming_Tech.text:
Shane Lowry is the first player to be traded in the TMRW Golf League (TGL) and will join Rory McIlroy at Boston Common Golf for 2027.

Ireland's Lowry makes the move before the third season of TGL, which takes place at the SoFi Centre in Florida and comprises traditional golf with technology.

The 39-year-old spent the first two seasons at The Bay GC, and he will now link up with six-time major winner McIlroy as team rosters expand to five players for the new campaign.

USA Ryder Cup captain Keegan Bradley and Masters champions Adam Scott and Hideki Matsuyama joined McIlroy at Boston Common Golf last season.

In a trade for Lowry, The Bay will acquire Boston Common Golf's fourth draft selection to fill its open roster spot, as well as one future selection over the next three seasons and commercial considerations.

McIlroy, who co-founded TGL alongside Tiger Woods and Mike McCarley, said 2019 Open champion Lowry is a "great friend" and he loves playing alongside him.

"We've had some special wins together, including at the Zurich Classic, and I know the quality of his game and how much he cares about winning for his team-mates," he added.

"I'm delighted to welcome him to Boston Common Golf and excited about what we can achieve together this season."

Lowry, who won the Irish Open at Doonbeg in September, added he was "delighted" to make the move to link up with McIlroy for the new campaign.

"Having Rory alongside me and being part of this group makes it particularly exciting, and I'm looking forward to helping the team bring a championship to Boston," he said.

Elsewhere in the league, new team Motor City Golf Club announced five-time major winner Brooks Koepka as its first player.

Gaming_Tech.title: UK asks Apple to widen access to its payment tech
Gaming_Tech.text:
UK smartphone users could benefit from new payment, ticket and travel apps if Apple widens access to its contactless payment tech, the competition watchdog says.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) also wants the fees Apple charges firms to use its contactless tech to be "substantially lower".

It believes the iPhone maker's current fees and charges are "blocking" financial technology firms and others from innovating and growing - and is consulting on proposals it believes would cause these fees to fall.

Apple maintains that widening access could undermine security, and that its current arrangements do not stop innovation.

Nearly 2 in 5 payments are now contactless, the watchdog said, with nearly 60% of people using digital wallets - with Apple's the most popular in the UK.

In a statement Apple told the BBC that the current arrangements had permitted developers in the UK and around the world to securely offer contactless transactions directly within their apps, for everything from in-store payments and transit passes to car keys and event tickets.

"This solution enables developers and banks to create innovative products and services for their customers and facilitates competition between wallets, while ensuring users' sensitive data remains protected by the highest security standards".

"We do not believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an approach with lower privacy and security protections. We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome that is in the best interest of our users."

Last year Apple warned UK regulators against following the same path as the EU which forced it to open up a range of its technologies to rivals.

However, the CMA argued that, unlike the EU, it is focused on ensuring the interoperability of particular aspects of Apple's tech, such as digital wallets and watches.

The proposed measures would force Apple to grant access to apps that make payments via a widely used alternative contactless technology standard, called Host Card Emulation (HCE), which the firm does not currently permit in the UK.

Gaming_Tech.title: Uber wins bid to throw out £340m lawsuits from black cab drivers
Gaming_Tech.text:
Uber has won its bid to throw out claims worth about £340m brought by thousands of London black cab drivers and two former private hire firms.

The claimants alleged the ride-hailing company gave Transport for London (TfL) misleading information when it first got a licence to operate in the capital in 2012.

But a High Court judge ruled the cases had been brought too late and dismissed them without considering whether the allegations were true.

Uber, which denied the claims, said it was pleased the court had thrown them out at the earliest opportunity.

About 13,000 drivers were seeking nearly £200m in damages, Reuters reported, while a claim on behalf of Kabbie and Iride, two private hire firms that have since closed, sought about £140m.

The lawsuits were filed in 2024, and Uber argued they fell outside the six-year limit for bringing such claims.

In a written ruling, Mr Justice Birt said the claimants could have discovered the alleged deception before 2018.

RGL Management, which ran the cases for the claimants, said it was very disappointed and was considering its options with the legal team.

Since gaining its licence, Uber has taken much of the trade once dominated by black cabs.

The company faces a separate case next week, when it challenges HM Revenue and Customs in a tax dispute worth more than £1bn.

Gaming_Tech.title: China economy: Growth accelerates as AI export boom outweighs domestic weakness
Gaming_Tech.text:
China's economic growth picked up in the three months to the end of September, rebounding from a three-year low as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom helped boost exports.

The world's second largest economy grew by 4.5% in the third quarter, up from the previous period but below the 5% expansion recorded from January to March, according to official Chinese data.

The latest figure is at the bottom end of Beijing's annual growth target of 4.5%-5%, which analysts have said gives policymakers room to address the country's economic challenges.

While exports have helped offset weak spending at home, global trade tensions and uncertainty over AI investments are clouding its outlook.

China's National Bureau of Statistics said on Monday that the economy "sustained steady development against pressure" and showed "momentum with new growth drivers and improving structure".

With exports climbing, China's trade surplus - the amount of goods and services it sells abroad compared to what it buys from other countries - is on track to overtake the record $1.2tn (£900bn) seen last year.

Sales of high-tech goods rose by 14.3% while the production of both batteries and industrial robots grew by more than 29%, official figures showed.

Oxford Economics researcher Sheana Yue said manufacturing and high-tech exports have boosted China's growth, despite weak investment and domestic spending.

But property investment fell by more than 20% in the first nine months from the same period last year, official data also showed.

China's economy has been struggling to shake off a long-running property slump, after years of overbuilding and excessive borrowing by private developers.

There are still no signs that this trend will end soon, Yue said.

Trade uncertainties and geopolitical issues have also made Chinese consumers more "pessimistic" and unwilling to spend, she added.

Gaming_Tech.title: No further action against government adviser's wife over Palestine Action post, police say
Gaming_Tech.text:
Police say no further action will be taken against the wife of the government's national security adviser after she posted on social media referencing Palestine Action.

Sarah Helm, who is married to Jonathan Powell, wrote on X on Thursday: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."

She was responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support the proscribed organisation.

On Saturday, the Metropolitan Police said Helm's post was "assessed by specialist officers and it was determined that it did not meet the criminal threshold".

"No further police action will be taken," the force added.

On Friday, the Met Police had said it was "in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required" after it was "made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action".

Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025. Support of the group is a criminal offence and punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

Best-selling author Rooney said she would donate earnings from her books to the group, which has a stated goal of "ending global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime".

As a result, Rooney's publisher, Faber, determined it could not sell her novels, including Normal People and Conversations with Friends, in the UK.

Gaming_Tech.title: Social media algorithms: What if you could turn them off?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder

Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.

It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.

Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.

Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.

It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.

He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.

"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."

The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.

Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."

Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.

Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.

But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.

Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.

While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.

"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.

More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.

"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.

"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m).

"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.

The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.

Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.

"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external.

On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.

The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.

The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.

Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global.

"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."

Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.

Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."

Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.

Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice.

"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."

If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

Gaming_Tech.title: Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested
Gaming_Tech.text:
German police have detained a Russian man accused of being part of a cyber-crime gang which caused chaos at London hospitals and contributed to a patient's death.

The hack of blood testing company Synnovis in 2024 led to disrupted pathology services across several London hospitals and was the first cyber attack in history to be directly linked to a death.

The BBC can confirm German detectives are now including the incident in their investigation into the detained Russian and his associates.

Separately, the BBC has learned that British police are examining whether its own inquiry may lead to an unlawful killing case - potentially a world first in cyber-crime.

The detained suspect is a 28-year-old Russian man named by German press as Vladimir K.

He was arrested in Japan in May when he travelled to the country for a holiday.

According to German officials, the suspect's holiday plans were intercepted and he was arrested by Japanese police when he entered the country.

He is accused of being one of the core members of the Qilin cyber-crime gang - which has allegedly hacked more than 4,000 organisations since 2024 and extorted more than $140m (£105m) from victims.

Vladimir K was wanted in Germany for hacking into a logistics company in September 2024, encrypting data on its systems and extorting it for around $160,000 in cryptocurrency.

While his extradition was first reported in early October, external, the BBC can now confirm German police are including the Synnovis hack in their investigations.

Synnovis is diagnostics and pathology service which operates as a partnership between the hospitals and German company Synlab.

A critical incident was declared at some London hospitals after the provider was targeted by Qilin on 3 June 2024, with blood transfusion services severely disrupted, operations cancelled and emergency patients diverted elsewhere.

King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, one of two trusts heavily impacted, confirmed a year after the hack that one patient had also "died unexpectedly".

A spokesperson for the trust said a number of contributing factors led to the patient's death including "a long wait for a blood test result".

"The patient safety incident investigation identified a number of contributing factors that led to the patient's death," they said at the time.

A similar attack in 2020 by a different hacker group on a hospital in Düsseldorf in Germany led to a negligent homicide investigation being opened after an elderly patient died.

It was later dropped after medical experts concluded the patient's condition was so severe that they would have died regardless of the issues caused by the cyber-attack.

Prosecutors could also not definitively prove that it was the direct cause of death.

In total, the Synnovis hack in 2024 disrupted more than 10,000 appointments and caused weeks of disruption.

The hackers also threatened to publish the data on their dark net website unless Synnovis paid a ransom.

Gaming_Tech.title: Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram grooming becoming 'quicker and easier'
Gaming_Tech.text:
Experts are urging parents to talk to their children amid warnings social media grooming is becoming "quicker" and "easier" than ever before.

Childline said Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram were the top platforms children named in counselling about online sexual abuse last year. The companies have been approached for comment.

Avon and Somerset Police's child exploitation prevention officer Andri Nicolau said children as young as five can be targeted through social media, gaming and messaging platforms. She urged parents to encourage kids to ask for help without fear of blame or punishment.

The warning comes after three men were jailed for grooming a 17-year-old girl on Snapchat before raping her.

Research by the NSPCC found sexual communication offences involving children in the South West have more than doubled since the offence was introduced seven years ago, to 756 in 2024/25.

Of those, 300 were recorded by Avon and Somerset Police, 96 by Gloucestershire Constabulary and 61 by Wiltshire Police.

The charity also said Snapchat was mentioned in 324 counselling sessions about online sexual abuse between April 2025 and March 2026, a 19% increase on the previous year.

TikTok (234) and Instagram (197) were the next most frequently mentioned platforms.

Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the NSPCC, said: "It's deeply disturbing that hundreds of children have come to us in the past year alone, disclosing experiences of online sexual abuse linked to these popular apps and platforms.

"These crimes are highly distressing for victims, often leaving children and their families to deal with devastating lifelong impacts."

Another recent example involved Suleman Aqeel, from Speedwell in Bristol, who was jailed for 17 years at Bristol Crown Court on 30 September.

Aqeel used social media, including Snapchat, to arrange to meet young girls. He also filmed some of his offences and threatened to share intimate videos and images.

New data suggests that this particular form of exploitation of children, known as 'sextortion', has also reached record levels.

The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) said there has been a sharp rise in the number of young people contacting its confidential Report Remove helpline, external because they fear sexual images of themselves have been shared, or could be shared, online.

Criminals try to extort or blackmail their victims by threatening to publish the images, which have often been taken by the child themselves.

Nicolau said children spending more time online meant they were increasingly vulnerable to grooming, which is "easier" and "quicker" than ever before.

"With online gaming and social media, you have kids from five years old online, some of them have their own phones, so it can be any age," she said.

She works with schools to inform children how to be safe online, but said they are often unaware of the risks, including not viewing people they meet online as strangers and expecting them to be "nasty" from the start.

Nicolau encouraged any child or young person who believes they are being groomed to "find someone they are comfortable with and speak to them".

She said the police might not be the first choice, but speaking to somebody they trust is what mattered.

Nicolau urged parents to talk to their children and not take away devices or ban them from platforms, warning this could make them feel they were to blame.

"Sit down with your child, tell them it's not their fault, even if they've sent indecent images of themselves," she said.

"Believe them and give them the authorisation to say whatever they need to say."

Ella Bradshaw, the NSPCC's policy and public affairs officer, advised parents to start conversations about online safety as early as possible so that children know that they have a "safe adult" to go to.

"Often, particularly if it's to do with grooming or any kind of sexual or romantic relationship, children can be really scared of being judged and embarrassed to talk," said Bradshaw.

"Making sure that your child knows that you will stand by them, that you will respond with warmth and care rather than judging them or blaming them for what's going on is really important."

James Simmons-Read, who leads the Children's Society national exploitation prevention programme, said there are "huge concerns" about the growing scale of child sexual abuse and exploitation online.

"Perpetrators are always adapting ways they can better reach young people, whether that's through gaming or social media," he said.

He said another worrying trend was young people turning to AI rather than adults for advice and support about online harms.

Simmons-Read urged parents to normalise conversations with young people about their online lives.

Simmons-Read said the social media ban for under 16s, which is due to come into force in 2027, "doesn't go far enough", could be bypassed by criminals and could even discourage young people from speaking up about online grooming.

"We want tech platforms to invest more in detecting exploitation when it's happening on their platforms," he said.

A government spokesperson said it was preparing legislation to make it impossible for children to take, share or view nude images on their devices, which would make the UK the first country to do so.

"Alongside this, tech companies must be part of the solution and meet their legal and moral obligations. Where they fall short, the government will not hesitate to step in," the spokesperson said.

Kerry Smith, chief executive of the IWF, said: "We welcome the commitment to introducing nudity blocking technology on children's devices – but there really is no time to lose."

Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, said it is working to "fight and prevent grooming in a range of ways".

A Meta spokesperson said: "This includes restricting contact between adults and teens they're not connected to, and using technology to find and remove known child exploitation imagery.

"We also use behavioural signals to identify accounts showing possible signs of grooming or a sexual interest in children.

"Based on the strength of the signals, we either prevent them from finding and following teens or we remove their account completely."

Snapchat and TikTok have all been approached by the BBC for comment.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

Gaming_Tech.title: Sir Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr back new Beatles attraction
Gaming_Tech.text:
Sir Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr have backed plans for a major new Beatles visitor attraction in Liverpool.

The development will see The Beatles Story move from Albert Dock to the former St John's Market site, alongside a new Yellow Submarine experience at St John's Beacon.

McCartney said he "can't wait" for people to be able to "step into our story", while Starr said: "Liverpool was, and still is, Music City".

The attraction will feature immersive technology, original artefacts and recreated sets charting the band's rise from post-war Liverpool to international fame.

Apple Corps Ltd, which manages The Beatles' creative and business interests, will take over operation of The Beatles Story in 2027 ahead of its relocation the following year.

The attraction has been based at Albert Dock since 1990. Under the plans, it would move to the former St John's Market Hall, vacant since the market closed in 2024. At 100,000 sq ft, the new site would be more than four times the size of the current attraction, while the former Radio City tower, St John's Beacon, would house a new Yellow Submarine experience.

Announcing the plans, Apple Corps chief executive Tom Greene said Liverpool was getting a Beatles destination worthy of the city's musical heritage.

"Just like Graceland or Dollywood, it's fitting that The Beatles will have a world-class destination for fans to visit in the city where the story started," he said.

Apple Corps said visitors would be taken on a journey from the band's post-war Liverpool roots through Hamburg, The Cavern, Beatlemania, Abbey Road, Shea Stadium, Savile Row and beyond.

Commenting on the announcement Sir Paul McCartney said: "I love Liverpool. It's part of who I am, it's part of who The Beatles are.

"I find it incredible and humbling that people are still interested in our story and it's very exciting to me that The Beatles Story and The Beacon are being transformed in such an exciting way in the heart of Liverpool city.

"It couldn't have happened without Liverpool and I can't wait for people to be able to step into our story and share the experience."

Tickets sold for The Beatles Story will contribute to the The Apple Corps Liverpool Trust, a charitable initiative to provide support and opportunities for emerging local artists.

Ringo Starr said: "Liverpool was, and still is, Music City.

"And now we are expanding The Beatles Story Experience in Liverpool - how far out. The beat goes on.

"I also love that proceeds from every ticket will go back to support new Liverpool artists. It is great to be part of this. Deep down I am still a scouser. I love what Apple Corps and Liverpool are doing."

The project is a partnership between Apple Corps, Liverpool City Council and Liverpool City Region Combined Authority, with support from central government.

Liverpool City Region Mayor Steve Rotheram said it felt right that the "definitive Beatles experience" should be located in the city where the band's story began.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "The Beatles are one of the greatest examples of what Britain can give to the world.

"Four young men from Liverpool changed music and popular culture forever and, more than 60 years later, their story is still a source of enormous pride for this city and for our whole country."

Reflecting on what his bandmates would have made of the plans, Sir Paul McCartney said: "If you'd told us this was going to happen when we were hanging out and getting started, we'd never have believed it."

Gaming_Tech.title: Google cloud failure hits millions as UK courts and banks knocked offline
Gaming_Tech.text:
An outage at Google’s cloud services in the UK has caused widespread disruption, hitting courts and leaving millions of customers unable to access or send cash at banks including Lloyds, HSBC and Revolut.

Google blamed a “power event” for the failure at its London-based Cloud computing operations on Tuesday, which affected its “europe-west2-b zone”.

The US tech company said services were starting to come back online as of 1pm London time, and were back online for most customers by 3pm, but not before critical financial transactions and legal proceedings were disrupted.

That included the video system used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely across England and Wales, which failed to work throughout the morning.

The issue was believed to have delayed several hearings, as the system is often used for defendants who are in custody, but need to attend court.

Meanwhile, bank customers at high street lenders and leading digital bank Revolut were left in limbo through the first half of the day as services including card payments, cash withdrawals and transfers were disrupted.

The City regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, confirmed it was in touch with Google and seeking more information about the outage.

Halifax, owned by Lloyds Bank, said on X that some of its customers had been unable to log in via the app and online.

Revolut said its app was down because of a “service disruption” affecting several services, but insisted that customers’ funds and data were safe. The outage was affecting new and current customers, hitting its sign-up, sign-in, card payments, transfers, ATM withdrawals and cryptocurrency services.

In a statement, Revolut said: “We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”

A spokesperson for Lloyds originally said that customers were having issues with “certain online services” on Tuesday morning but that they were aware of “similar issues affecting other organisations”. By the afternoon, the banking group issued an update saying: “We understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect to all our services back to normal soon.”

HSBC customers had also been complaining online that they were struggling to access their accounts. A spokesperson for the bank said: “We are aware that some customers are experiencing difficulties accessing our services. We would like to apologise for any inconvenience and continue to monitor the situation, which is also affecting other organisations.”

This outage will be the first major test for the FCA and Bank of England, since the City watchdogs were handed powers to regulate Google and other rival services that have been supplying “critical” cloud services to UK financial firms this summer.

The property portal Rightmove was also reportedly affected by the Google cloud outage, and NewsThump, the satire and spoof news website, was struggling to load. Reports suggested Royal Mail and DPD had also suffered disruption.

Google said: “We will publish an analysis of this incident once we have completed our internal investigation. We thank you for your patience while we’re working on resolving the issue.”

Gaming_Tech.title: The dangers of letting tech billionaires shape our world
Gaming_Tech.text:
Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while sitting in front of Roy Lichtenstein’s monumental Drowning Girl, on view in New York City. Today in tech, we’re discussing the perils of Elon Musk’s one-man global infrastructure, AI-generated music, and a Guardian AI conference in Paris.

Elon Musk’s orbital ownership

Elon Musk’s SpaceX is the single largest satellite operator in the world, larger than any government space bureau. The life-threatening consequences of that dominance and centralization of power are on full display. One man is in charge of global, vital infrastructure, which is thumbing the scales in the war on Ukraine.

SpaceX’s internet service was throttled in Ukraine amid a series of devastating attacks by Russia last week, leaving the country extremely vulnerable. The US government controls StarShield, the satellite internet service produced by SpaceXSI for the Pentagon, which is what Ukraine relies on. Objects moving faster than 100 mph (160.9 km/h) – drones, the centerpiece of Ukraine’s counteroffensive – lost connectivity. The sudden restrictions Tuesday evening led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions. Russian drones fly at nearly 200 mph (328.9 km/h), so Ukrainian interceptor drones can’t catch them without Starlink, and no alternative is as yet viable. In response, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky warned “people will die.”

The cutoff comes alongside Donald Trump’s mercurial souring on Ukraine. Pressured domestically by the high price of diesel and upcoming midterm elections, the US president has eased sanctions on Russia, and Zelensky has said US intelligence agencies on several occasions in recent days didn’t warn Ukraine of incoming missile attacks, as they usually do. Musk has denied his own involvement in StarShield’s malfunctioning, writing, “This is not under SpaceX control.”

Reuters reported that the request to throttle the service in Ukraine came from the White House. Responding to the claim, Trump said: “I don’t know if it was anybody because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon. And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.” US secretary of state Marco Rubio said “no one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down the internet.”

Entertainment.title: BBC closures make business sense, but far more savings are needed, says Katie Razzall
Entertainment.text:
The BBC's announcement that it will close three of its linear broadcast channels - BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra - makes sense financially.

BBC Three's most popular show on Monday night was a repeat of an old episode of Top Gear. Around 77,000 people tuned in.

BBC Scotland's TV channel was watched, according to this year's annual report, by a weekly average of 12% of the Scottish population. Scots simply aren't tuning in in the numbers to make it cost-effective.

(Fascinatingly, BBC Alba, which is aimed at Gaelic speakers and learners, reached 43% of Scots weekly - was it boosted by its rights to broadcast Italian football's Serie A, with the commentary mainly in Gaelic?)

It's hard to argue - although no doubt some will - that there is a business case for keeping BBC Scotland's TV channel open.

The same goes for BBC Three, although the hokey cokey that has gone on with that channel - launched to fanfare in 2003, later made digital-only, then brought back to linear in 2022, now back online only again - has looked indecisive. Bizarre even.

But the bigger picture is that viewers and listeners are already migrating online - increasingly finding the BBC's programmes not via those linear TV and radio channels but on iPlayer, BBC Sounds, and, more recently, YouTube.

So that's the business case - and the BBC needs to save £500m over the next three years. That figure is concentrating minds.

But axing the three linear channels is a drop in the ocean financially. I understand it will save less than £10m in total per year.

Last year the BBC spent £42m creating content for BBC Scotland. It still plans to create many of those shows for iPlayer - and BBC Two in Scotland will be reconfigured to deliver Scotland-only programming.

The part of BBC Three that commissions programmes will actually get more money to spend on creating content aimed specifically at 16-34s (with a core focus on the 16-25s).

This was the network that commissioned Normal People, Fleabag, Killing Eve - programmes of quality and wide appeal.

There's also been a recent announcement of commissions dreamt up specifically for YouTube - to reach those 16-24s who the BBC (and other public service broadcasters) find so difficult to lure to their own platforms.

Many of Radio 4 Extra's programmes will also still be on BBC Sounds. If you listen to the Daily Service, first broadcast in 1928 and the longest-running programme of its kind anywhere in the world, you will still be able to find it.

So these aren't major cost savings. The BBC would likely argue, when it comes to audiences, who are at the heart of everything, it is pivoting to find them where they already are.

What's been announced today is more about the direction of travel. It's about the continuing evolution of the BBC, a streamlining as audience habits change.

That doesn't mean it isn't painful to all of us inside the BBC. Job cuts are always difficult. In News, 100 more roles are being axed. That's on top of the 200 already announced. And the news division is still nowhere near its target of £51m of cuts.

And with only two fifths of the £500m of total savings now announced, there is still a very long way to go.

As a BBC user, you are going to hear much more about cuts in the coming months. Some will think that is a good thing as the BBC reflects the belt-tightening going on in most homes and companies across the UK. Others fear that the BBC's important role in public life is being chipped away.

There is a bigger fight going on here. The BBC is negotiating with the government over its future - and how it will be paid for. It won't harm the negotiations if it can show the corporation is being streamlined and made more efficient.

As long as it can also demonstrate that audiences aren't being left behind.

Entertainment.title: Esther Rantzen felt 'deprived of choice' over her own death
Entertainment.text:
A posthumous note written by Dame Esther Rantzen said she was "deprived of any choice over my own death".

The farewell message was released as the 86-year-old broadcaster and campaigner's family confirmed she had been laid to rest in an "incredibly beautiful" private funeral last week.

The Childline founder, who was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer in 2023, died at her Bramshaw home in the New Forest, Hampshire, on 30 September.

A larger memorial service is expected to take place at a later date.

Rantzen's daughter Rebecca Wilcox said the family had been inundated with messages since her death.

"It's been hugely comforting to know that people around the world felt the same way about her as we did," she said.

Dame Esther became a prominent campaigner for assisted dying in her later years, something MPs voted against legalising in September.

In her note, she wrote: "It would have transformed the way I died if the law had allowed me to ask for assistance to die when my life had become unbearable.

"I was extremely lucky because I had the talent, skill and support of my local Oakhaven Hospice.

"But I was still deprived of any choice over my own death by the current messy criminal law."

She said she had become "too physically frail to take the flight" to an assisted dying clinic in Switzerland.

Entertainment.title: Alice Cooper on character, church and drugs ahead of Wolverhampton appearance
Entertainment.text:
Rock legend Alice Cooper has opened up about his redemption arc from the stage to the church ahead of a book tour pit stop in Wolverhampton.

"It's such a strange life that I had because I was the prodigal son. I grew up in a Christian church, went as far away as you can, then came back," he told BBC Radio WM.

It comes after the singer-songwriter published his autobiography, Devil on My Shoulder, earlier this month, detailing the highs and lows of his nearly six-decade career that earned him the title of the Godfather of Shock Rock.

He is set to appear at the University of Wolverhampton at The Halls on Tuesday.

Known for hits such as School's Out, Poison and I'm Eighteen, Cooper, whose real name is Vincent Damon Furnier, spoke about the stark difference between himself and his on-stage alter ego.

"Alice, the character I play on stage, couldn't be more opposite to me.

"All through the book, I'll say something and the character will come in and go, 'Wait a minute, that didn't happen like that', so I'm arguing with my character - the Jekyll and Hyde thing all the way through the book, which is kind of unique," the 78-year-old said.

He added: "I love playing him because that's who he is and he should be that on stage, but off stage we don't think alike at all.

"I'm in church on Sunday. I even teach Bible study sometimes and you would look at the character on stage and go 'how can that be?'"

The rock star also spoke openly about the dangers of drugs and alcohol and warned that today's young people face a far more dangerous environment than previous generations.

"When I was on cocaine, I was an entirely different person. All of my senses went away and I was living for the drug, so it's a form of possession," he said.

"And same with alcohol. I know people who are the nicest people in the world but, as soon as they drink, they become just the opposite. It's almost a poison or an allergy or something."

The singer spoke about Solid Rock, an organisation he launched to support young people by offering free after-school training in music, dance and art.

"I think kids are living in a really dangerous world right now. What's going on on the street is a much more dangerous world than what we had.

"The drugs that are on the street right now will kill you very quickly, whereas in our day, if you got caught with a joint or got caught with a beer you were in trouble if you were underage. Now it's heroin, that's a big jump.

"In the 70s, when we were going, it was normal. In fact, it was unusual if you weren't doing it. Now, we've all learned from all the people who died at 27 that it doesn't work."

During his trip to Wolverhampton, there will also be a Q&A session for fans to engage with the star.

The event will be the last of eight dates on the UK book tour, which has also included Cardiff, Cambridge, Brighton, Manchester, Stockton-on-Tees and Glasgow, as well as the London Palladium.

Entertainment.title: Christiane Amanpour: CNN reporter and anchor to leave network after 43 years
Entertainment.text:
CNN's chief international anchor, Christiane Amanpour, has announced she will leave the organisation next year after more than four decades.

"After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!" Amanpour said in a statement., external

The 68-year-old said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral".

CNN chairman Mark Thompson described her as "one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere" and said the network will take time to celebrate her "before she departs next year".

Amanpour began working for CNN in 1983 as an assistant on the international news desk, and went on to become one of the network's best-known correspondents, often reporting on conflicts and wars.

She has presented her own nightly interview program on CNN International since 2009.

Entertainment.title: Kylie Jenner makes Victoria Secret debut in $50 million bra
Entertainment.text:
Reality TV star Kylie Jenner has sparked mixed reaction after making her Victoria's Secret Fashion Show debut in a $50m (£37m) bra.

The make-up mogul surprised the crowd at the lingerie giant's annual show on Sunday while wearing the famed Fantasy Bra, which was made of 18-carat gold and 4,410 diamonds, according to the designer.

The Fantasy Bra has been a key feature of the show over the years and wearing it is typically seen as an honour and defining moment for the chosen model.

The Kardashians star, 29, being selected to wear the piece delighted some fans, while many others criticised the brand for not giving the opportunity to a veteran supermodel.

Social media and marketing expert Joel Marlinarson says the moment was well-engineered and generated "a lot of conversation" on what it means for the "future of modelling and social media".

"Of course Kylie represents a new era of celebrity where brands are prioritising who's going to bring the most eyeballs, as opposed to who fits the cookie cutter definition of a model," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

Marlinarson says young viewers have a connection with Jenner having grown up watching her on social media and through her reality show with her Kardashian sisters.

However, he says there will be a section of the audience who remembers "the iconic Naomi Campbell era of fashion" who might see Jenner being given this moment as a "betrayal of what they know".

"Ultimately, this represents this new era of marketing where brands, particularly Victoria's Secret and legacy brands, they don't want to take risks," he says.

"They want to bring in somebody who they know is going to generate eyeballs, who's going to generate those headlines and who can consistently raise a crowd and that's exactly what Victoria's Secret has done."

Some fans cheered on Jenner in the comments of a video shared on Victoria's Secret Instagram page unveiling the dramatic look., external

While many others branded it as "pure disrespect to real models" and questioned why she was picked out of a "room full of talented models".

One said the show has "gone from iconic glamour to an influencer circus" and they felt "social media clout and performative inclusivity have replaced real modeling talent, elegance, and runway presence".

Chief creative officer at Victoria's Secret, Adam Selman, told Vogue, external that Jenner was picked for being a "cultural powerhouse".

"Kylie really extends beyond fashion, beyond culture, beyond TV, beyond one singular thing," he adds.

"That's the exact same thing that we do.

"Like, the show is so big, it's true entertainment, and I think that she is a great catalyst for that."

Entertainment.title: Unseen Only Fools and Horses clips from Margate to air in documentary
Entertainment.text:
Previously unseen footage from a much-loved episode of Only Fools and Horses will reveal more depth and texture to the characters of the classic British sitcom, the maker of a new documentary has said.

Only Fools and Horses: The Lost Archive will show previously cut clips from a number of episodes including The Jolly Boys' Outing, filmed and based in Margate.

Richard Latto, a comedy archive specialist who unearthed some of the material, said it showed how well written the characters were and he hoped the scenes could be used in extended episodes.

He told the BBC the Jolly Boys' Outing footage "was absolutely amazing to find" and he remembered watching it with his family on Christmas Day.

Latto added: "The episodes are so well known, so to now have scenes that aren't so well known that are still incredibly funny made it special.

"I think people will see much more depth and texture to the characters, and learn a bit more about them."

Latto said much of the newly-found content was scenes which had been removed to meet time restrictions, but were still of good quality.

Entertainment.title: Selena Gomez says vaping has affected her voice
Entertainment.text:
Selena Gomez has said vaping nicotine has changed the way her voice sounds.

"I'm not gonna be able to change my voice," the singer, 34, said in a candid Instagram post, external on Sunday. "I vaped nicotine a lot."

"Nicotine is so hard to quit and I just wanted to say, if you're going through it, or if you're even trying to vape, it's just not worth it," she continued.

"It's so stupid and it changed my voice," she reiterated, then laughed: "So if you guys don't like listening to my voice, that's totally understandable. I don't mind. Just don't listen to it."

The singer and actress, who has the chronic autoimmune disease lupus, has previously suggested that the condition was affecting her vocal cords.

Asked about her voice in an Instagram Q&A last December,, external she said: "Sometimes things happen. I get weird. My throat kind of swells inside sometimes. That's all."⁠

Lupus flare-ups can cause inflammation around the larynx (voice box), which can cause your voice to become raspy and strained - similar to the symptoms of a cold.

Gomez's voice has also deepened with age, which is not uncommon. However, some fans have fixated on the change, posting compilation videos showing the evolution of her speaking style, external on YouTube.

In her Instagram video, the Only Murders In The Building star noted she had recently weaned herself off nicotine.

"I am really excited because I stopped and I just hope I can keep it up," she said.

"It's really hard, but I know if you are going through something you can get through it too. It sucks."

Entertainment.title: Jury in Katie Price ex's rape trial told to ignore egos
Entertainment.text:
Jurors in the rape trial of Katie Price's ex-husband have been told to cut through the "big egos" and "big personalities" involved in the case before considering their verdicts.

Kieran Hayler, 39, is on trial at Lewes Crown Court charged with three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault of a 13-year-old girl in West Sussex in 2016, which he denies.

In a closing speech on Monday, prosecutor Ryan Richter told jurors: "You've seen the whirlwind of what is Katie Price and you're going to make an assessment of her, how it affects this case, how much it helps you decide.

"The prosecution accept you're likely to treat her evidence with caution."

Richter added: "You may well put 90% of her evidence to one side, it's irrelevant, it doesn't help you.

"I'm sure you will concentrate on what is relevant and look for support to assess what she says."

The prosecutor said jurors had seen enough of "the egos, posing and posturing".

"You've seen the big personalities, the big egos in this case, and you'll judge it, you'll cut through it," he said.

"You'll decide whether those big voices drown out the voice of [the complainant] or whether that voice has made you sure on the counts of this indictment."

Referring to messages between the alleged victim and Price in 2017 where the media personality told the girl "I will make you a little star", Richter asked: "Is that the key to this case, that message?"

He added: "Is it the suggestion seriously for nine years Katie Price has been biding her time to make [the complainant] a star?"

Defence barrister Arlette Piercy said in her closing speech that Hayler had been consistent and clear throughout his defence in what had been a "rollercoaster ride for everybody in this court".

She called for the jury to take care, be calm and rational, warning "emotion is enemy of reason".

Piercy pointed to inconsistencies in the complainant's evidence that on more than 30 occasions she said she did not know or could not remember.

"We submit lack of coherent account is an important factor which supports what we are saying and undermines the credibility of the witness as a whole," Piercy said.

Hayler denies all the charges against him and says the allegations are a "smear campaign to ruin me" by Price.

The trial continues.

Entertainment.title: Clayface's Tom Rhys Harries says prosthetics helped performance
Entertainment.text:
Actors are often said to be the face of the film, but in Tom Rhys Harries' breakout role in DC's latest blockbuster, that part of the body becomes the focal point to chart the character's descent into villainy.

Rhys Harries plays the lead in Clayface as Matt Hagen - a handsome, successful actor.

When his face is mutilated in an attack, he volunteers for trials of a new treatment with horrifying side effects that transform his face into living clay.

The Welsh actor said he spent about half of his time on the set with the special effects make-up team, transforming into the mutant villain.

Despite the difficulty of wearing extensive prosthetics during filming, Rhys Harries said it helped him portray the distress of his character in a film that has been described as a body horror psychological thriller.

"There was a benefit to having it, because the character is in discomfort," he said.

Clayface first appeared in DC comics in 1940 as a Batman villain, however the character has never been adapted for cinema, until now, and it is the first major studio movie role for Rhys Harries.

"Time will tell if I'm prepared for it," the Cardiff-born actor said.

"I think it feels like a real privilege to be allowed into that sandbox, it's a cultural thing that is fairly significant in the West certainly.

"So I just feel really grateful to be able to put my stamp on Matt and Clayface for the first time."

Where possible, the creative team used malleable physical effects to better reflect the consistency of a clay-like substance, something Rhys Harries said was a "steep learning curve".

Entertainment.title: ‘We’ll keep doing this if people pay us!’ The cast of TV hit Ghosts on making a movie – and maybe a caveman spinoff
Entertainment.text:
When the final episode of Ghosts was aired in December 2023, the sitcom felt as if it had reached a definitive conclusion. The show’s central relationships, between Charlotte Ritchie’s Alison and the ghosts who haunt her tumbledown inherited manor house, were neatly tied up, as they encouraged her to sell the place to a hotel developer. It was a tearjerker of an episode for the millions of people who watched it, as well as for the cast and crew behind the scenes.

“We had stopped the series with genuinely no intention of coming back,” explains the show’s co-creator Mathew Baynton, who also stars as the callow romantic poet Thomas. “We were all in tears on the last day of filming,” he says, now perched on the uncomfortable end of a chaise lounge in a London hotel suite.

“I was so upset that it finished,” adds Lolly Adefope, who plays the excitable Kitty, from the better structured end of the chaise. “It was like being at a party and you guys were leaving.”

“It was a clear ending, and the guys felt like they had fully explored all of the characters,” says director Simon Hynd, “but I did notice a look of regret in some of their eyes.”

All of which is to say that Ghosts is now back. Although the television series remains over, the story will continue in the new film Ghosts: The Possession of Button House. So the question is, who blinked first?

“Alison Carpenter, our executive at Monumental, had started to say, ‘We could get the funding for a film if you guys want to do that,’” explains Baynton. “But we just batted it away.”

“The fear was that you’d end up making a 90-minute episode of a TV show, and it would feel like, Please Sir! The Movie,” says co-creator and star Laurence Rickard, who plays both caveman Robin and decapitated nobleman Sir Humphrey Bone. “Which I love, by the way.”

Eventually Carpenter convinced the show’s six creators and stars (the others being Simon Farnaby, Martha Howe-Douglas, Jim Howick and Ben Willbond, not present) to at least get into a room and discuss the prospect. “We all talked through what we didn’t want it to be, and what it sort of had to be to be a film,” explains Baynton. “That led us very quickly to the concept of possession, which would allow one of the ghosts to get out of the grounds.”

“It was the fastest turnaround ever,” laughs Rickard. “We went in at 9:30am going ‘I mean, it’s nice to see everyone, but I think the answer is probably no’ – and then by 11 o’clock, we were going, ‘We have to do this.’”

The resulting film is still very much Ghosts, with its unique mix of sharp absurdity (at one point a Ouija board spells out ‘Leave’ to make a point about Brexit) and near-debilitating emotional notes (you may never again look at a scotch egg without crying). But it is undoubtedly a movie, with stakes and a ticking clock and big set pieces.

“The possession idea immediately invites a body swap sort of thing, which reminded us of Big,” says Baynton. “Then we were talking about, what if the possession doesn’t last and his spirit is fading, which reminded us of Back to the Future. The group of kids breaking into the house felt like The Goonies. All our touchstones for this were films we loved in our youth.”

The film is an astonishing feat, not just because of its quick turnaround – Hynd only learned of the film late last year – but because every member of its ensemble has a vital part to play in the plot.

“With the series, we got so used to writing multi-thread narratives,” explains Baynton. “In any episode, the actual stories are told in two or three brief moments, so that had become our mode of writing anyway.”

This approach meant that, despite no longer living in Button House, Alison and her husband Mike, played by Kiell Smith-Bynoe, find themselves swept up in the action. Smith-Bynoe seems especially pleased with his arc. “Mike gets to prove himself in this one,” he explains, “which felt good after spending a few years not getting to do that.”

Smith-Bynoe has arguably always had the hardest acting job on Ghosts, as Mike is often the only person on screen who isn’t a ghost and can’t interact with them. This challenge was doubled for the film’s climax when, without giving too much away, a roomful of characters old and new flit in and out of tangibility. “It took me a minute,” he says. “I had to keep asking Simon who I was supposed to be able to see.”

Much of the cast this time around are new, in the form of the aforementioned kids. It takes a lot to steal a film out from underneath a cast as talented as this, but Scott Ellis Watson, who played the young John Davidson in I Swear, is phenomenal here, largely because he spends a lot of time doing a bang-on impersonation of a dead middle-aged Tory MP.

The new additions were something that Adefope in particular appreciated. “It was so fun having Scott around,” she says. “I was sort of the Gen Z member of the cast, so we talked a lot about memes and TikTok.”

“You were the child whisperer, weren’t you?” says Rickard.

“Yes, exactly. I was translating for you,” she smiles back.

With the show, the six creators were able to break off and write individual episodes in various permutations of their troupe. But the film is credited to all six of them. Was that a hard thing to accomplish? “It was just a process of who was around at what time,” says Baynton. “So sometimes it was two of us, sometimes three or four. What is lovely about that is that the person who’s absent for a little period of time then becomes your fresh pair of eyes when they return. You get to a point at times where all you can see is A or B and both of them are problematic, but then someone who’s been away for a couple of weeks comes in and goes, ‘Well, what about C?’ And you go, ‘Oh yeah!’”

A lot of this is simply muscle memory. The Ghosts team are now veterans, having met while making the Horrible Histories TV show almost two decades ago, and continued with the sitcom Yonderland and the 2015 Shakespeare comedy film Bill. It’s hard to think of any writing and performing group this large who have managed to stay intact for so long. Even Monty Python ran out of films and shows in less time, their work together now largely consisting of tweeting hatred at each other.

“Oh, we’ve got that phase to look forward to,” laughs Rickard. “I’ve been drafting some of that stuff.”

Rickard is the one who seems to have most keenly felt the absence of Ghosts: “The first year after the series stopped was the first time that we hadn’t done something together in 18 years.” You get the sense that this film exists in part because its creators missed hanging out with each other.

So why stop the party now? Will there be anything else to look forward to from the gang? “There isn’t something secretly being developed,” insists Baynton. “But we’ve always had the same feeling, which is that we love working together and we’ll keep doing it if people will pay us to do it.”

Does that mean more Ghosts films? That prompts a slightly more uneasy response. “This does sort of feel like, you know, the big swan song,” replies Rickard.

“Yes, but we said that before, so no one can take our word for it,” adds Baynton. “But there’s no intention. Also, ghosts can’t age, and I’m rapidly getting way too old to play Thomas.”

“But Robin could definitely have a spinoff, and that wouldn’t be a problem,” cracks Rickard, noting that he’s looking more and more like a long-dead caveman with every passing year. “It would be great. My makeup call would get shaved right down.”

Entertainment.title: ‘I had no plan. Just total scorched earth’: how Kiran Leonard survived teen success to make songs of full-body joy
Entertainment.text:
Kiran Leonard presses the tips of his fingers together and looks at me solemnly across the table. “I don’t know if I’m doing a very good job,” he says, “But I’m trying really, really hard not to swear.”

A decade ago, he explains, he was interviewed by the Guardian, got too drunk, and “swore all the way through the interview”. When the piece came out, his grandfather was thrilled. “But he couldn’t show any of his friends because I just sounded really aggressive,” he tells me sheepishly.

It’s true that, the last time Leonard had a profile in this paper, he sounded a lot like a twentysomething trying hard to shed the preciousness of his former status as a teenage wunderkind. Hailed as a prodigy at age 16, upon the release of baroque, bonkers 2012 debut Bowler Hat Soup, a lot of Leonard’s early press plays up his age in a way that now reads as embarrassingly trite. “I think, unconsciously, I was probably quite defensive about how I was written about,” he says. “It’s not nice for journalists to fetishise the density or the ambitiousness of the music – it [was] obviously meant in a slightly patronising way.”

The Leonard sitting across from me at a pub near his home in south-east London speaks calmly and carefully, like someone with nothing to prove – because, perhaps, he has so thoroughly proved himself over the interceding decade. In the past five or so years, Leonard has emerged as one of Britain’s most consistently fascinating experimental musicians. His recent slate includes 2024’s Real Home, a rangy pop record that touches on ramshackle country, menacing prog and Jonathan Richman-esque romanticism; last year’s Small Brown Bed/With You Waltz, a surrealist album of live takes recorded at notable DIY venues such as the Golden Lion in Todmorden and Delicious Clam in Sheffield with a group of musicians he calls No Tailgate; and credits on acclaimed records by Eli Winter, Caroline and My New Band Believe.

His music is certainly far less wordy these days, far less likely to garner comparisons to Captain Beefheart or Joanna Newsom. But that’s because at this point, he says, he’s searching more for a sense of pure feeling: “I’m strongly driven by a very physical thing – which might seem quite broad, but it’s what distinguishes what I’m interested in and what I’m not.”

Leonard was born and raised in Saddleworth, near Manchester, the son of a community midwife and John Leonard, a folk musician who worked for BBC Radio 1 and 2 in Manchester in the 80s and 90s. Although it’s clear he was making music from a young age, it’s less clear how he ended up signed, with a manager and booking agent, before he could legally drink. “The short answer is: I don’t know,” he says. “I was very ignorant and sheltered from a lot of it. I made Bowler Hat Soup and put it on Bandcamp. I think I sent it to a load of blogs, and a blog wrote about it, which was then read by [the people who ran the label] Hand of Glory. I didn’t really come up through like, gigging.”

From there, Leonard was set up with that dreaded industry mechanism: a team. He got a publicist and a radio plugger and, through his management, a band, thankfully comprised of Manchester musicians who were at least making music that felt aligned with Leonard’s own. “I was fortunate to work with really good people and great musicians and have all this support, but the context was wrong,” he says.

During that period, he made and released four albums, but increasingly felt as if he wasn’t in the right zone. Enamoured by fuck-the-industry icons such as Steve Albini, he began tanking his commitments because the music was the one thing he had control over. He moved to London and then, one day, ditched his entire team. “It was a disaster – just total scorched earth,” he says with a sheepish smile. “I had no plan, had no idea what I was doing.”

Leonard found London “really alienating and difficult”, a feeling that was compounded by the fact that, he soon realised, he didn’t really know how much his team had sheltered him. “I couldn’t really find another manager – never have since, actually. And couldn’t get gigs,” he says.

Leonard “gradually found a groove in London, found a way to find it really stimulating and engaging”. That came through booking more shows and from befriending the post-rock band Caroline, who are the nexus of some of the country’s most vital experimental music. “I’m sure many people in this community would say the same thing,” he says. The band have become “a centre of activity in a lot of the work that I do because there’s so many of them, the quality of what they do is such a high standard and they’re operating at a level that everyone is very proud of and impressed by.”

Leonard quickly realised that his work could comprise “different investigations” – that he didn’t have to feel pinned down by one style, and that he didn’t have to be haunted by the music he made as a teenager. “I wanted to articulate myself more clearly and with less pomposity, less adolescent over-the-top-ness,” he says. “With the teenagery records, a lot of them were coming out much later than they’d been made. The difference between 15 and 18 is really massive, so playing those songs, I’d feel a bit of a dissonance, which made me more conscious of wanting to move past [them].”

Leonard says that most of his work now is extremely solitary, although he occasionally plays in Caroline, and enjoys playing in a project where he doesn’t have to add his own compositional voice to the mix. An exception to that solitary work is Or Sobre Blau, Leonard’s duo with Catalan guitarist Andreu G Serra. Their remarkable second album, Making Friends, released earlier this year, is a heady mix of ambient guitar primitivism, oddball samples and scratched-up found sound. “Or Sobre Blau is really thrilling because it’s in a totally different voice,” he says. “It’s the voice of that friendship, which is really thrilling because for my stuff, I’m just in my head, which is sometimes horrible.”

If there’s a common link between all Leonard’s work now, it’s that it often comes from a desire to make sounds that conjure full-body sensations. He often gets there. “I remember having a conversation with someone about the Caroline song Total Euphoria,” says Leonard. “They were like, I don’t know how often I feel total euphoria. I’m like: ‘I feel it quite a lot.’”
