articles.title: The singles choosing IRL dating events over apps
articles.text:
Checking in at a dating event in a bar in Guildford, Olivia Miller-Davis is understandably apprehensive.

Even bringing a friend with her doesn't remove the awkwardness at the start of the night.

"It's always nerve-wracking when you're meeting new people," the 28-year-old admits before downloading an app that will match her to other daters based on their star signs.

This is speed dating 2026-style and Olivia, like many people we speak to, is here because she's fed up of "endlessly swiping" or as some describe it "app fatigue".

She says she hates judging people with "really limited information and just a couple of pictures" because she doesn't feel she can "really fully commit" with so little to go on.

According to a recent study from online regulator Ofcom 11% of adults use dating sites but it suggests the time we spend on them is dropping, from a peak of almost four hours a month in 2023, down to three hours last year.

Olivia's first match on the night is Edward and he agrees that recent dating trends leave him feeling cold.

"I'm fed up with apps," he says.

"I mean, they're designed so that you don't find 'the one', because they want you to come back and use the app forever. They don't want you to get married from the app."

The event is organised by Love at First Sign, a dating company that uses an app to match people based on astrological connection, but most people are just using it as an icebreaker.

Director of events Lissy Cleminson says the way people date is changing and a big factor is more home working since Covid, which means people do not meet in offices or on the commute.

"The little meet-cutes don't happen so much when you're at home with your shirt up top and your pyjamas down bottom," she jokes.

Those running apps are quick to point out online is still a big part in the way people meet.

New research from Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, suggests that out of those who had ever had a romantic relationship, about 21% of baby boomers surveyed met their most recent partner at a pub, bar or club.

Among Gen Z, it was just 4%.

The survey of 3,007 single people also suggests that of those who had ever had a relationship, 20% met their most recent partner on a dating app and 20% met through friends.

Chine Mmegwa, head of strategy, corporate development and operations at Match Group, says Tinder has made tweaks to its service in the past year to win back younger daters.

As well as helping users find out more about each other in advance of dates, through interactive music and astrology features, it has introduced "double date mode" for friends who want to date together.

And Tinder is doing more to encourage people to connect IRL, she says. "They want to be in person. You've seen us launch events across the US and now the UK. We are bringing IRL experiences into the app.

"What we're doing is putting IRL into our experience. And so we are bringing that gap to what they're looking for in person, using the apps."

In Guildford, Olivia says her night was a success because she met some men she might want to go on a first date with.

When pushed by the BBC on whether she thought she had met "the one", she laughs and becomes understandably guarded.

"No, I'm not going to name anyone specific. But you'll be invited to the wedding if there is one!"

articles.title: What is the Budget and what could be in it?
articles.text:
The run-up to the Budget typically generates speculation about what might be in it, which the government is trying to keep to a minimum this year.

Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending, while also sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules.

The previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, set out two main rules, which the new leadership has vowed to follow. These are:

In March, the OBR calculated that the first rule would be met with a gap - or headroom - of £23.6bn. However, this headroom is expected to have shrunk.

Analysts are divided on how much it may have fallen by. While a rise in government borrowing costs will increase debt interest payments, higher inflation could push up tax revenues.

KPMG believes the government's buffer could have fallen to £12bn, but the Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates it could be £20bn.

There has been speculation over what specific measures will be announced in the Budget.

Bank bosses have told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.

The Treasury has options: it could raise a 3% surcharge on profits which was lowered from 8% under the previous Conservative government, or it could raise the bank levy that is based on the size of their balance sheets.

Your First Home scheme

Further details on the Your First Home scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property, are expected to be announced in the Budget.

The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

There had been speculation that Capital Gains Tax (CGT) - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value - could be changed, through either higher rates or by removing or amending exemptions. However, this has now been ruled out.

The Times has reported, external that online retail giants such as Amazon and eBay are expected to be made responsible for collecting tax owed by traders using their platforms.

The paper said the money raised is expected to be used by the government to cut business rates for High Street shops, by raising the threshold at which small companies start paying rates from £12,000 to £18,000.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

Healey told the BBC in late September that the time and place for dealing with rising petrol and diesel costs was the Budget, but would not give details on whether the freeze would be extended again.

Household energy bills are set to see their biggest rise in four years in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276.

There has been speculation, external that Healey is planning energy bill help for households on certain benefits.

The High Value Council Tax Surcharge - dubbed the mansion tax - was announced in last year's Budget and will apply to properties in England valued above £2m from April 2028.

articles.title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
articles.text:
President Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs.

Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world."

While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households.

The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up.

So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims.

The overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards.

The latest data shows US GDP, external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%.

And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term.

That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period.

The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025.

It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending.

Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy.

The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country.

Spending on building data centres, external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office.

Many American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic.

The current rate of US inflation, external is 3.7%.

That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025.

Economists estimate, external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office.

While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation.

The price of a gallon of diesel in the US, external - a fuel used not only by drivers but also widely in agriculture and industry - hit a record high of $6.52 in September.

The price of some grocery staples , externallike beef and coffee have risen since Trump returned to office, though the price of eggs has fallen.

And some US retailers have warned, external that rising energy prices caused by the Iran war will make producing food more expensive and raise prices at the till.

Average US household incomes are still rising under Trump.

The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record, external.

However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following, external on US households:

- Trump's tax cuts

- The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans

- Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran war

ITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off.

The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts.

ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank, external.

The growing deficit is also one of the reasons the US government gets charged more to borrow money in financial markets.

The 10-year US government bond yield has risen sharply since Trump returned to office in January 2025 and is now above 5%, the highest rate since the global financial crisis in 2007.

That increase in the market cost of US government borrowing also puts upward pressure on the interest rates on mortgages available to American households.

The interest rate on a new 30-year US mortgage has risen to 7.4%, external per year, up from 6.9% when Trump returned to the White House.

That's added to problems in the US housing market, making homes less affordable for new buyers. It has left many existing owners reluctant to move because doing so would mean giving up their cheaper mortgages, which they took out at lower rates, external and cannot take with them to a new property.

articles.title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
articles.text:
Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France.

The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".

Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend.

"The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said.

Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.

More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).

Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage.

Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses.

Those that stole goods now appear to be looking to sell them on fast.

"Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," Vinted told the BBC.

"When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans."

France is one of Vinted's largest markets, along with the UK and Italy.

The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour".

eBay has not noted any increase in listings linked to the looting in France, but said it works with law enforcement to investigate suspected stolen goods and takes appropriate action, including removing listings and taking action against sellers, when authorities confirm an item is stolen.

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support, claims prosecutors
articles.text:
A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.

US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the ChatGPT-maker, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and said a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.

The 35-year-old engineer was deemed a flight risk and denied bail on Monday, pending a trial.

The Saudi government did not respond to BBC requests for comment.

Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.

The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.

A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.

The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.

It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.

Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.

On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.

"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.

US district judge Alex Tse on Monday denied Alfozan's attorneys request for his release on bail, saying "there is a risk of non-appearance that is significant".

The FBI investigation is ongoing.

Alfozan was scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine.

articles.title: Musk and Anthropic pledge share giveaways
articles.text:
Elon Musk's SpaceX and artificial intelligence giant Anthropic have pledged big financial giveaways as Big Tech firms come under pressure over the potential impact of AI on humanity.

Musk said on Monday that he would give one of his shares at his rocket company, which owns xAI, to every child in America next year.

The billionaire's announcement came after Anthropic said it would commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".

Anthropic is laying the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn). SpaceX set the record for biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history in June, raising $85.7bn.

The pledges come at a time when the AI industry is under intense scrutiny over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and jobs.

Details over how each American child would be handed a share in SpaceX have not been disclosed.

In a post on social media,, external Musk said: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many."

It came after he responded to Anthropic's public fund pledge with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public. This is what I will be doing."

Anthropic said none of the shares held in its Public Benefit Fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas.

The Claude developer said on Sunday that the fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion.

Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.

In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.

Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.

Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI, with that figure rising as high as ​60% in advanced economies.

In September, a researcher who quit Anthropic said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.

Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.

The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, had previously called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document, making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

Trump has repeatedly rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.

articles.title: Google Cloud outage: problems fixed for ‘most‘ customers, as regulators push for details – latest updates
articles.text:
Google Cloud outage: A summary

A power outage at a Google Cloud data centre near London has caused serious failures to services today, affecting operations for several UK banks.

Problems were first detected just after 7am this morning, disrupting “multiple services” in Google’s europe-west2 region (London).

Google blamed the problem on a ‘power issue’ – just afternoon today it said this event had been mitigated. By 1pm UK time services were recovering, and at 3pm Google said services were back online for most customers, with only “a very small number” still affected.

But by that time, millions of customers had been left unable to access and send cash at banks including Lloyds, HSBC and Revolut.

double quotation mark“We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”

A spokesperson for Lloyds added:

double quotation mark“Our app is online and customers can log in normally, though we understand some are having issues with certain online services this morning. We are aware of similar issues affecting other organisations and are monitoring the situation closely.”

Legal proceedings were disrupted, because the video system used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely across England and Wales which failed to work throughout the morning.

The City regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, confirmed it was in touch with Google and seeking more information about the outage.

This outage will be the first major test for the FCA and Bank of England, since the City watchdogs were handed powers to regulate Google and other rival services that have been supplying “critical” cloud services to UK financial firms this summer.

Tech experts said the outage was another reminder of the dangers of relying on a small number of technology providers for cloud services, a year after problems at Amazon Cloud caused more widespread disruption.

Reynolds: Chinese EV decision will depend on UK interests

Business secretary Johnny Reynolds has insisted any decision to impose tariffs on Chinese EVs will be about British, not EU interests.

He told the business select committee that some were under the misapprehension that the EU wanted the UK to put tariffs on EVs because they feared the Chinese could use Britain as a “backdoor” to the bloc, circumventing trade defence measures including tariffs on EVs and quota on electric hybrid cars.

He point out that this Chinese cars exported from the UK “would not qualify” for duty free exports to the EU under the rules of origin clauses in the Brexit trade and cooperation agreement”.

He was also asked about last week’s Franco-German paper proposing that the UK would be included in the upcoming Made in Europe legislation on condition London aligned with EU trade defence measures.

But he said the “detail” of that proposal, which has yet to be adopted by the EU in any new drafting of the Industrial Accelerator Act, “has not been surfaced to the degree to which we’d be able to definitively say that that is what the ask is of the UK.”

Google Cloud outage: A summary

A power outage at a Google Cloud data centre near London has caused serious failures to services today, affecting operations for several UK banks.

Problems were first detected just after 7am this morning, disrupting “multiple services” in Google’s europe-west2 region (London).

Google blamed the problem on a ‘power issue’ – just afternoon today it said this event had been mitigated. By 1pm UK time services were recovering, and at 3pm Google said services were back online for most customers, with only “a very small number” still affected.

But by that time, millions of customers had been left unable to access and send cash at banks including Lloyds, HSBC and Revolut.

double quotation mark“We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”

A spokesperson for Lloyds added:

double quotation mark“Our app is online and customers can log in normally, though we understand some are having issues with certain online services this morning. We are aware of similar issues affecting other organisations and are monitoring the situation closely.”

Legal proceedings were disrupted, because the video system used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely across England and Wales which failed to work throughout the morning.

The City regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, confirmed it was in touch with Google and seeking more information about the outage.

This outage will be the first major test for the FCA and Bank of England, since the City watchdogs were handed powers to regulate Google and other rival services that have been supplying “critical” cloud services to UK financial firms this summer.

Tech experts said the outage was another reminder of the dangers of relying on a small number of technology providers for cloud services, a year after problems at Amazon Cloud caused more widespread disruption.

Google: We'll publish an analysis of what went wrong

Google add that it does not plan to provide further updates about the outage on its Service Health page – another sign that it thinks it has pretty much resolved the problem with its cloud services today.

double quotation markWe will publish an analysis of this incident once we have completed our internal investigation.

We thank you for your patience while we’re working on resolving the issue.

Google: issue has been mitigated for most customers

Newsflash: Google has declared that it has won, pretty much, its battle against today’s tech outage at its London-based cloud computing systems.

In an updated status message, Google says:

double quotation markMultiple services were experiencing issues in the europe-west2 region.

The shift to the past tense is significant – until now, the messages said that services “are” experiencing issues.

Google then declares that all but a few customers have now been helped, saying:

double quotation markThe issue with impacted GCP products has been mitigated for most of the customers and it is believed to be affecting currently a very small number of customers and our Engineering Team is working on it.

If you have questions or are impacted, please open a case with the Support Team and we will work with you until this issue is resolved.

Royal Mail has said it was aware of the issues caused to its services by the Google Cloud outage, and added that there was no effect on letter and parcel deliveries.

Not that those deliveries are always good enough!

Businesss secretary Johnny Reynolds has said he has summoned Royal Mail bosses in for talks to discuss changes to improve the services, my colleague Lisa O’Carroll reports.

He told a parliamentary business committee that the Royal Mail is not delivering “the level of service people expect”.

Royal Mail have not met their first or second class standards for almost 10 years, the committee heard.

Reynolds said the government had negotiated the take over by Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský last year which included a curb on dividends “until performance improved”.

“I know for parliamentarians this in oral questions on Thursday and other correspondence with members of Parliament that it is one of the most significant issues they’re facing,” Reynolds told the committee.

He said the government “recognised the need for regulatory reform” but Ofcom was taking a lead at the moment on this subject.

double quotation mark“I am going to have Royal Mail and the unions in for a conversation about this. I need to respond to what MPs are being told.

“Royal Mail is a really important institution and business, and I know it has significant ramifications when it’s not hitting the levels of service. And I can promise you, chair, whether it’s work with Ofcom, whether it’s work with, with, you know, any part, any key player, any stakeholder in this, we will do what we can to make sure Royal Mail is the service it needs to be.”

Lloyds: expect services to get back to normal soon

Lloyds Banking Group, which includes Halifax, is hopeful that services will be restored soon.

A spokesperson for Lloyds tells us:

double quotation mark“We understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect to all our services back to normal soon.”

UK regulators want answers from Google about Cloud outage

Kalyeena Makortoff

The Financial Conduct Authority and Bank of England are pushing Google for details of today’s cloud services outage, as they face their first major test as new regulators of “critical” tech suppliers to UK banks.

Both the FCA and Bank of England were handed powers in July to start directly overseeing the local arms of Google Cloud and three other Silicon Valley rivals - Amazon Web Services, Oracle and Microsoft – after being designated as critical third parties by the UK government, as their services become a crucial part of increasingly digital banking services.

A spokesperson for the FCA said they were in touch with Google and seeking more information about the outage. The Bank of England’s Prudential Regulation Authority is also understood to be speaking with the tech firm about the service outage which began this morning (details start here).

The watchdogs are in charge of ensuring that the cloud providers are resilient and actively reducing the risk of cyber-attacks and major outages like the one experienced today, which has disrupted services for millions of people and businesses across the UK.

For its part, Google is meant to prove it is carrying out proper stress testing, including how it would respond to imagined emergency scenarios that would put their operations under severe strain. They’re also meant to have reported any major incidents, including this power outages, to the two regulators (though it’s unclear in what time frame).

Updated at 09.30 EDT

Low-paid workers and hospitality firms face disruption

The failure of banking apps due to the Google Cloud outage could disproportionately affect those most struggling with the cost of living, argues audit, tax and business advisory firm Blick Rothenberg.

Blick Rothenberg partner Andrew Sanford explains:

double quotation mark“Weekly or fortnightly paid employees, often those on lower wages, may have found that they are unable to access their funds on the very day where they have payments or commitments to make.”

“The hospitality sector will also be disproportionately impacted by those people affected by the outage with no means of making payment, who simply do not go the pub or restaurant.”

Affected companies coming back online again

There are signs that the companies affected by Google’s outage are getting online again.

Emma, the personal finance, budgeting, and money management app which was taken down by the Google Cloud outage (see 10.11am), has posted on X that it is operating again.

double quotation markWe’re back ✅ Emma is up and running again after this morning’s Google Cloud power outage in London. Your data and money were safe throughout. Some balances may take a little while to refresh. Thanks for your patience 💜

Google: We are seeing the recovery of services for most workloads

Newsflash: Google says service ​are being ‌restored ‌in its London-based ‌cloud region after today’s outage.

double quotation mark“We are seeing the recovery of services for most workloads in europe-west2.”

This isn’t the end of the story, though – Google are promising another update by 3pm UK time.

Updated at 08.51 EDT

Google added that they will provide an update by 06:00 PDT (2pm BST) with “current details” of the situation.

Google: The power event is mitigated

Newsflash: Google says the ‘power event’ which affected its London-based cloud computing operating and caused widepread disruption to services in the UK has been ‘mitigated’.

In a new statement on its Service Health page, Google reports seeing signs that services are being restored.

double quotation markA power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. We are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritizing the recovery of existing workloads.Customers may not be able to yet create new workloads.

Full recovery of existing workloads should be completed, tentatively by Tuesday, 2026-10-20 06:00 [Pacific Daylight Time].

[CORRECTED: 6am PDT is 2pm UK time.]

Updated at 09.32 EDT

The Google Cloud outage could result in some companies losing sales, and they might struggle to get much compensation, suggests Ryan Gracey, partner at law firm Gordons.

double quotation mark“Many businesses will be discovering today that their cloud contracts protect the supplier far more than they protect the customer.

“When a provider goes down, the usual remedy is a modest credit against future fees. That is small consolation set against lost revenue, frustrated customers and damage to reputation.

“Liability for those wider losses is typically capped or excluded altogether. The real exposure sits in the gap between how heavily a business depends on its provider and how little its contract actually guarantees. For banks, the stakes are higher still. Regulators expect them to keep essential services running even when a key supplier fails.

“Outsourcing a service does not mean outsourcing responsibility for it. Boards should be asking, not just what their contracts promise, but whether the business could keep going if its provider went dark for a day.”

Google: power event disrupted our Cloud services

Google are blaming a ‘power event’ for the disruption at its London-based Cloud computing operations today.

In an update on its status page, Google says:

double quotation markDue to a power event we had suffered an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. Partial mitigation to infrastructure services will be observed within the next 30 minutes and the remaining services will be mitigated there after.

PA: Court hearings delayed as nationwide video system goes down

The video system used by courts across England and Wales went down on Tuesday in an issue believed to be linked to the wider Google outage, the Press Association report.

The Cloud Video Platform (CVP), which is used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely, was not functioning throughout the morning.

Users expecting to attend court on video link were met with a message saying there was an internal server error.

The issue is expected to have left many hearings across the country delayed or unable to go ahead as the system is often used for defendants who are in custody to attend court.

The judge in the Russell Brand trial, Mr Justice Bennathan, decided to press on with proceedings at Southwark Crown Court on Tuesday morning despite the link being broken.

Some journalists who would have been watching online were squeezed into extra seats in court, but many were not able to follow the proceedings as the fourth complainant started her evidence.

Staff at the court said there was a national outage and did not know when it would be resolved.

It is understood to be linked to an outage affecting Google’s Cloud network, which affected businesses including online bank Revolut, delivery service DPD and Royal Mail.

The nature of cloud ecosystems mean that a problem in one region can ripple out and cause widesread disruption.

Dr Amro Al-Said Ahmad, lecturer in computer science at Keele University, explains:

double quotation mark“Another outage, another reminder of the fragility of cloud infrastructure. Google Cloud is currently experiencing a major incident affecting the europe-west2 (London) region, with elevated errors and intermittent network failures impacting more than 38 cloud-native services across key categories including Compute & Containers, Storage & Databases, Analytics & Data Processing, Networking & Connectivity, Messaging & Streaming, Caching & Memory Services, and AI/Platform Services.

“Google Engineers are actively investigating the issue and testing mitigations, including moving impacted workloads to alternative regions where feasible. The disruption has also affected several major organisations and financial institutions that rely on the affected region.

“More importantly, the incident highlights the dependency effect of modern cloud ecosystems. When a core cloud region experiences failures, the impact extends far beyond the directly affected services. Applications, APIs, databases, authentication systems, payment platforms, analytics pipelines, and third-party SaaS products that depend on those services can all experience cascading failures.

“A problem in a single cloud region can therefore propagate through an entire digital supply chain, affecting organisations that are several layers removed from the original outage. While this is a regional outage centred on europe-west2, the breadth of affected services highlights a key cloud engineering lesson: resilience is not achieved by simply moving to the cloud. True resilience requires designing for regional failures through multi-region deployments, workload portability, and tested disaster recovery procedures.”

A Lloyds spokesperson has confirmed the bank (which includes Halifax) has experienced problems today:

double quotation mark“Our app is online and customers can log in normally, though we understand some are having issues with certain online services this morning. We are aware of similar issues affecting other organisations and are monitoring the situation closely.”

Google’s latest update on its Cloud outage reiterates what we knew already.

double quotation markWe apologize to all who are affected by the disruption.

Multiple Google Cloud services are experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region.

Note: Looker Studio is not impacted by this outage.

If feasible, the impacted customer may try to migrate their workload impacted to another available location (zone or region).

Updated at 07.05 EDT

articles.title: Paddy Power cuts 1,400 jobs and blames betting tax rises
articles.text:
Paddy Power-owner Flutter has announced plans to cut up to 1,400 jobs as its boss claimed the company "cannot fully absorb" tax rises imposed on the gambling industry.

Staff based in Leeds and Dublin, as well as workers for its UK and Ireland business at Flutter's Portugal and Romania sites, will be most affected, but what roles are at risk has not been disclosed.

The government announced taxes rises on online casino and sports betting, with an exemption for horse racing, in the Budget last year.

Flutter boss Kevin Harrington said the tax hikes had "fundamentally changed" the economic model of the UK betting and gaming industry, arguing it had helped "fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market".

"We continue to expect these tax increases to have a very significant impact on the overall market," Flutter Entertainment said on Tuesday.

Flutter, which also owns Sky Bet and Betfair, employs 28,500 people across the world, including 9,000 in the UK and Ireland.

As well as its Leeds and Dublin offices, the BBC understands the cuts could also affect staff based in London and Sunderland, as well as Malta and Gibraltar.

Harrington, who is chief executive of the betting giant's UK and Ireland business, said: "As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future."

A government spokesperson said the job cuts were a "commercial decision for Flutter, not the UK government".

"However, we understand this will be a difficult time for the workers," they added.

Flutter delisted from the London Stock Exchange in August in a blow to the UK, with its shares now solely traded in New York.

In its most recent results, the company reported a $299m (£224m) pre-tax loss for the three months to June for its entire business worldwide, compared to a $205m profit in the same period last year. Sales rose 3% to $4.3bn.

However, revenues in the UK and Ireland rose by 4% over the period, due to strong growth in online gambling games.

Some online gambling tax rises announced in last year's Budget took effect in April. This included remote gaming duty, which is paid on online casino betting, rising from 21% to 40%.

General betting duty, paid on the profits made from various forms of sports betting, was kept at 15% in betting shops, but is set to rise from 15% to 25% online in April next year.

Betting firms had warned that cost increases would lead to job losses and betting shop closures, but MPs dismissed the warnings as "scaremongering".

During the summer, Ladbrokes owner Entain announced job cuts, with news agency Reuters reporting 500 roles were being removed.

Punters' winnings from gambling are not taxed in the UK, nor is VAT charged on bets.

Flutter said its restructuring plan would cost between $80m and $90m.

The company has claimed in previous financial results that the impact of UK tax rises would hit its underlying profit by $320m this year and $540m in 2027, before any savings or restructure to mitigate the impact.

articles.title: Pakistan vs England: Sloppy visitors floored by Arafat Minhas in Rawalpindi
articles.text:
One-day international tri-series, Rawalpindi

Pakistan 302-9 (50 overs): Baker 3-65; Nawaz 79 (74), Arafat 59 (58)

England 215 (38.4 overs): Banton 57 (53), Arafat 6-40

Pakistan won by 87 runs

England began their wandering winter with a sloppy loss to Pakistan in the one-day tri-series in Rawalpindi.

In the opening match of five separate tours to four different countries on three continents, England's mistakes opened the door for Pakistan's Arafat Minhas to take advantage.

The all-rounder made a crucial 59 with the bat, then bamboozled England by taking 6-40 with his left-arm spin.

Asked to bat, Pakistan were 190-5 in the 37th over when diving wicketkeeper Jordan Cox put down Arafat on 12, one of three catches England dropped.

Arafat, alongside a powerful 79 from Hasan Nawaz, lifted Pakistan to 302-9.

Faced with making the second-highest score to win an ODI at the Rawalpindi Stadium, England made a rapid start to the chase, only for further errors to let Pakistan back in.

At 91-0, Ben Duckett top-edged a pull to depart for 45 and, crucially, Tom Banton was caught for 57 when he shovelled Arafat's long hop to mid-wicket.

Arafat's fine all-round performance continued with a beautiful delivery to bowl England captain Harry Brook for five and Naseem Shah got one to keep low to bowl Joe Root for 33.

When Cox was lbw and Jamie Overton holed out, both off Arafat, England were floored. They spluttered to 215 all out, losing their last seven wickets for 50 runs, capped by a calamitous run out of Gus Atkinson.

Pakistan have two wins from two in the tri-series and are already on the brink of the final, while England next meet Sri Lanka at the same ground on Thursday, with both sides looking for their first victory.

Not only is this the beginning of England's winter – two trips to Australia and Test tours of South Africa and Bangladesh follow – but also the start of a long run-in to the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa next year.

This was the first of a potential 21 ODIs in preparation for the World Cup, the tri-series format designed to replicate the pressure and permutations of tournament cricket.

In fairness to England, they have improved in ODI cricket - winning their three previous series this year - and they were without three first-choice players in Jos Buttler, Jofra Archer and Jacob Bethell.

Nevertheless, this was a game they could have won had they not wasted their opportunities, while squad players missed chances to press their case. Cox dropped two catches behind the stumps, Sonny Baker was expensive with the new ball and Banton squandered the platform to make a huge score at the top of the order.

The outcome was a defeat in their first ODI in Pakistan since 2005 and a loss in their first taste of tri-series ODI cricket since 2015.

To focus on England's shortcomings would be a disservice to Pakistan, who are a vastly different proposition in this format on home soil to the team soundly beaten in the Test series in the UK last month.

From 133-5 in the 28th over, the hosts could have wilted, yet Nawaz's slog-sweep for six from the first ball he faced from Adil Rashid was the beginning of Pakistan's fightback.

Along with Arafat and Faheem Ashraf, Nawaz carried Pakistan to what seemed no more than a competitive total on a flat pitch.

When night fell, Arafat produced his magical spell to the delight of a noisy full house.

He produced the best figures by a Pakistan spinner in an ODI against England, then Arafat also ran out Atkinson to complete the hosts' win.

This was a good test for England's batting, not unlike the kind of chase they can expect to face at the World Cup, albeit in different conditions.

Much like when they were tasked with overhauling 325 to beat Sri Lanka at Headingley in an ODI less than a month ago, they fell short.

Banton made a century in that series but knows the injured Bethell will be back for the tour of Australia next month. Another hundred would have made the selection decision difficult, explaining Banton's obvious disappointment when he somehow belted Arafat to Shaheen Afridi.

Cox will have a run in the ODI side because Buttler is out until at least the new year and the Essex man will also have an eye on securing a place in the Test team in South Africa.

At number six, Cox had the opportunity to make amends for his two drops, yet he was deceived by the wily Arafat to be lbw for 18.

In between, England lost their biggest wickets. Brook was all at sea in missing a beautiful turning delivery from Arafat, Root was arguably unlucky to be bowled by Naseem and Sam Curran, playing for the first time since The Hundred, shovelled to deep square leg.

When Curran departed for 27, England were 177-5 midway through the 32nd over and the game was beginning to slip away.

What followed was Arafat singled-handedly ripping through the lower order.

Cox was done in the flight to be leg before, Overton was caught at long-on and Will Jacks, so often England's saviour in white-ball cricket, found the hands of mid-wicket.

Rashid was palpably leg before and the mix-up between Baker and Atkinson that resulted in the latter face down on the turf epitomised England's collapse.

It was another chapter in England's long history of capitulating to spin on the sub-continent.

England captain Harry Brook: "We were quite happy with 300. We thought they were slightly under par. It got dewy as we thought it would do. We were pretty happy at halfway."

On not pushing on after a strong opening partnership: "That was the story of the innings. We thought [Tom] Banton, Ducky [Ben Duckett] set the tone to get a 100 partnership and then it was a case of losing too many wickets in clumps, we couldn't string the partnerships together and we ended up on the wrong side."

On where they will look to do better next time: "You always want to win, don't you? We've spoken a lot about rotation of strike through the middle but I think we were a little too careful against the spinners especially, so we can probably put them under a little bit more pressure in stages and we've got to tonight to talk about it and tomorrow and bounce back better on Thursday."

articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo let Manchester United down, says Erik ten Hag
articles.text:
Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag said Cristiano Ronaldo "let the team and let me down" during the Dutchman's spell at Old Trafford.

Portugal forward Ronaldo was in his second spell at United when Ten Hag took charge in the summer of 2022 but left in controversial circumstances a few months later.

"He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him," Ten Hag told The Athletic, external.

"I flew out to Portugal to speak with him about what I was aiming for before I came to United.

"Obviously, he's one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in."

Ten Hag had dropped Ronaldo for a Premier League game at Chelsea in October 2022 after he had refused to come on as a substitute against Tottenham three days earlier.

Ronaldo gave an interview in the November in which he said he felt "betrayed" by United, did not respect Ten Hag and was being forced out of the club prior to his departure being "mutually agreed".

Ronaldo was 36 when he returned to Manchester United from Juventus in 2021, when Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was manager.

Under Ten Hag, he scored just three goals in 16 outings before his exit during the 2022-23 campaign.

"It's the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he's exhausted," added Ten Hag. "But he couldn't. He ran neither in possession nor out of possession. The reason was because he didn't prepare himself.

"Every top team has to embrace the top player, but the top player has to work for the team.

"He was telling the players, 'save your legs at the training'. I understand it when you are top fit - you have sessions you can save the legs. But first you have to train yourself to get into the right fitness levels."

The publication of Ten Hag's interview comes as Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension and fined 255 euros (£215) by the Portuguese Football Federation for leaving his country's international camp last month.

Ten Hag was sacked by Manchester United in October 2024, having won the Carabao Cup in 2023 and FA Cup in 2024.

On his time at Old Trafford, Ten Hag added he wanted to sign Frenkie de Jong, Harry Kane and Declan Rice, and was against the sale of Scott McTominay to Napoli in August 2024.

"I said for the first season, 'centre-half, there's a problem, centre-midfield, there is a problem, and especially I need a strategist, then we need goals'. And that was the biggest issue in all my three years: goals," said Ten Hag.

articles.title: England rugby league: Brian McDermott names unchanged team for World Cup match against France
articles.text:
Brad O'Neill has dismissed the suggestion that England were underprepared for their Rugby League World Cup campaign as they bid to start salvaging it with an unchanged team against France this Saturday.

England are under pressure - and in huge danger of missing out on a semi-final spot - after losing last Saturday's opening match 30-12 to Tonga, but head coach Brian McDermott has kept faith with the same 19-man squad.

McDermott's side have had a tight turnaround for the tournament - the Tonga match was just 14 days after the 2026 Super League Grand Final, with England flying out to Australia 10 days before the game.

They did not play a warm-up match - and so went into the game having not played a single international fixture since losing to Australia in Headingley in November last year.

Defeat by Tonga came in McDermott's first match in charge since being appointed in April, and O'Neill said they are "new team" and "those little things should come together".

But when asked by BBC Sport if England were tired and underprepared for Tonga, the 2026 Super League Man of Steel said: "Not at all, we had a great week of prep heading into the tournament.

"The whole team felt really good physically, it was just a good game and the better team won."

England men: AJ Brimson, Dom Young, Hugo Savala, Herbie Farnworth, Zach Eckersley, George Williams, Harry Smith, Max King, Brad O'Neill, Luke Thompson, Junior Nsemba, Kai Pearce-Paul, Victor Radley.

Interchange: Jez Litten, Ben Currie, Ethan Havard, Sam Walters, Jack Welsby, Matty Ashton.

Reserves: Kallum Watkins, Mikey Lewis, Ben Talty.

McDermott had said he would "have a look" at team selection after Tonga, but has decided to stick with same XIII for this Saturday's match.

He also said England "were not strategically outdone" despite the heavy loss and only needed tweaks rather than a tactical overhaul.

"Only having a week together, those little things should come together and we should start executing with practice," said O'Neill.

"We're not changing anything we play, it is about the execution side of things. It is those combinations in training and bringing those to the match.

"There is a real belief in the team, we are a new team. We need time to work on combos, hopefully those will pay off."

That defeat, England's first ever against Tonga, has left McDermott's side with a tough task to reach the semi-finals.

Group B-C works as a combined pool of six teams, from which only the top two will reach the semi-finals. England, in Group B, are facing the three teams in Group C - Tonga, France and Papua New Guinea.

Qualification gets complicated if teams are level on points: Head-to-head record is the first tiebreaker - which would go against England if they finished level with Tonga. But points difference will be used if two teams in the group have not played each other - which would be the case if England and Samoa needed to be separated.

England must win their next two games, against France next Saturday and Papua New Guinea on 30 October, to stand a realistic chance of progression - and because of the World Cup's format, probably need to win them both by a big score.

Even then, there is the strong possibility that England will not know their fate for certain until two days after their final match, when Tonga face 2022 finalists Samoa in their last group game.

"We have discussed what is required, but we are taking it day by day," said O'Neill. "We are confident we can do it.

"We just focus on a game at the time and don't think much about format.

"Mentally we can't go in thinking about points, if we do our job well enough we will get the win."

In contrast to McDermott, England women's coach Stuart Barrow has made a big selection change before their blockbuster meeting with co-hosts Australia on Saturday.

Jenna Foubister will start at half-back, replacing Georgia Roche, after a superb year in the Super League where she was named Woman of Steel.

The 19-year-old, who scored on her debut in a 62-0 win against Wales in August 2025, will partner Izzy Rowe in the halves.

Rowe scored two tries and kicked nine conversions for 26 points as England opened their World Cup campaign with a 70-6 win against Wales last Saturday.

She equalled the record for the most points by an individual England player in a Women's World Cup match.

There are two other changes to the XIII, as Molly Jones replaces Georgia Wilson in the centres while Liv Wood plays at prop ahead of Mary Coleman.

Lucie Sams is named among the interchanges as England take on reigning champions Australia in Perth with kick-off at 10.05 BST - immediately after the men's match.

Australia coach Kevin Walters has dropped Reece Walsh to the bench for their second group game against Fiji on Sunday (09:05 GMT), with James Tedesco coming in at full-back.

Tedesco will also captain the co-hosts, as Isaah Yeo - who has delayed surgery on a torn pectoral muscle to play at the World Cup - is rested.

Walsh, who had not played since 15 August amid injury troubles, started as Australia were pushed by New Zealand in a thrilling World Cup opening match last Thursday.

He scored a try but kicked just two of five conversions as the Aussies squeezed to a 24-22 win at Sydney Football Stadium.

Tedesco steps up as one of five changes made by Walters. Bradman Best, Sam Walker and Blayke Brailey all come in for their Test debuts.

articles.title: Mark Allen: Former world number one considering retirement after Northern Ireland Open exit
articles.text:
An emotional Mark Allen said retiring from snooker is "something I have been contemplating for a while" following his first-round loss to Jordan Brown in the Northern Ireland Open.

Allen was beaten 4-2 by fellow Antrim man Brown in his first event since losing to Wu Yize in heartbreaking fashion in the semi-finals of the World Championship in Sheffield in May.

The former world number one said showing up to play his match against Brown was an "achievement" after a "really difficult" period in his life while he took a break from competitive action.

"I think if I hadn't have been playing Jordan, I probably would not have played," Allen told BBC Sport NI after his defeat at the Waterfront Hall in Belfast.

"I felt like I did not want my last match to be remembered for that semi final in Sheffield.

"I thought it would be a bit of nostalgia to go out playing Jordan in the Waterfront where it all started in 2005 and that would be a more fitting end if I do call it a day.

Asked if he is considering drawing the curtain on his career, he replied: "Yeah."

The 40-year-old has had a decorated career, winning 12 ranking tournaments including the 2022 UK Championship since he turned professional in 2005.

However, this year has been a challenging one for Allen after he missed a match-winning black in the semi-final against Yize in May during the penultimate frame that would have taken him into his first World Championship final.

Allen went on to lose the final frame of the against eventual champion Yize and has since been a notable absentee from the World Snooker Tour circuit.

"The last three months have been really, really difficult and I think even just being here today is an achievement," added Allen.

"For me, today was not about the result or the performance, it was trying to enjoy the experience of playing one of my best mates in one of my favourite arenas, in one of my favourite tournaments.

"I am not going to announce it [retirement] right now after a defeat but it is something I have been contemplating for a while and something needs to change within the next six weeks before the UK Championship for me to show up and I need to work hard on myself in the next few week and see what is around the corner."

articles.title: REDs: how relative energy deficiency in sport affects athletes
articles.text:
Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders

"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."

That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.

From the outside looking in, his career was flying.

By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.

But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.

Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.

After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.

It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.

The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.

But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.

BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.

REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.

Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.

"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.

"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."

Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".

Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs can have her periods "switched off".

For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.

The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".

But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.

"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.

"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."

Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.

Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.

So why is REDs so common?

One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.

For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.

And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.

"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.

"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."

Initially, the strategy can work.

When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.

It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.

But eventually, the luck runs out.

Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.

Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.

"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.

"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."

Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".

"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.

"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."

It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.

Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.

The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.

"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.

"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.

"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."

As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.

After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.

Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".

"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.

"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"

Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.

For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.

Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.

"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.

"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."

Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.

Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.

"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.

"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.

"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."

While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.

"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.

"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.

"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.

British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.

Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.

The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.

"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.

"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."

With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.

But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.

Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.

The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.

"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.

"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story you can visit BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Iga Swiatek: Six-time Grand Slam champion ends 2026 season after failing to qualify for WTA Finals
articles.text:
Six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek has called an early finish to what she described as "one of the most challenging" seasons of her career.

Poland's Swiatek failed to qualify for the end-of-season WTA Finals - for the first time since 2019 - after pulling out of the Ningbo Open on Tuesday with a thigh injury.

Shortly afterwards, the 25-year-old announced she was bringing a largely barren season to a close, in order to recharge over a longer period of time before returning in 2027.

Former long-time world number one Swiatek - who has ended a season without a Grand Slam title for the first time since 2021 - has dropped to ninth in the rankings.

"The past few months, or actually the past couple of years, have been incredibly intense," said Swiatek, who will have an opportunity to complete the career Grand Slam at the Australian Open in January.

"I feel I need to rest and recover my body fully, so that's exactly what I will do - [for] a bit longer this time."

Her most recent Grand Slam triumph came at Wimbledon last year.

Swiatek has managed one WTA title this season - the Canadian Open in August - and ends 2026 with a 42-16 win-loss record.

On Saturday, she lost to fellow Pole Maja Chwalinska in the Wuhan Open semi-finals, only her fourth defeat in 23 matches.

"I'm especially proud of the work we've done in the second half of the year and the progress that came with it," said Swiatek, who needed treatment on her thigh but played on against Chwalinska.

"It gives me a lot of confidence in what's ahead."
